English.Text: Sons Abroad
The Sultan sent our sons to the West to study railways and machines. Their letters speak of everything except railways and machines! Bring me one of them — I want to hear it from his own mouth.
Railways? Steam engines? Pah! Do you know how many kinds of cowrie shells live in the Gulf? Forty-three! I have catalogued every single one!
...and in the third act, the Sultan's daughter elopes with a stoker from London! The audience wept, I tell you!
My uncle sits in the Diwan of the capital. One letter from him, and your professor will be teaching geography in Wadi Al Zahir!
Forty-three seashells and not a single sketch of a locomotive! The Sultan paid for his passage to study railways!
A Sultan's daughter and a stoker! If the court hears of this play, we will all be posted somewhere even further away than Wadi Al Zahir — if such a place exists.
Threatening professors with his uncle's name... I shall write to the uncle myself. We shall see who ends up teaching geography in the desert.

To bring the industrial age to the Sultanate, the court has sent the sons of its envoys to study at the universities of the Old World. The Envoy has his doubts about their progress: their letters home are full of theatres, taverns and seashells, but strangely silent on engineering. He wants you to find them and bring back the one who most deserves a word with his elders.
The Envoy wants to check on the young Envoys studying in the Old World.
The students are holding forth in front of a crowd near the coast in the Old World
Choose one student and bring him back to Wadi Al Zahir
This student was sent to study railways — and collects seashells instead.
This student has abandoned the law for the theatre, and his plays would scandalise the court.
This student boasts that his uncle in the Diwan will protect him from any consequences.
The Envoy gives the young playwright a lecture he will never forget.
The Envoy is appalled at how the young man has spent his time abroad.
